### Identify the 18 genes included in the published T-cell–inflamed GEP and examine their expression in the dataset

18 genes included in the dataset

```{r}
#identifying 18 genes from dataset

GEP_genes <- c('CCL5', 'CD27', 'CD274', 'CD276', 'CD8A', 'CMKLR1', 'CXCL9', 'CXCR6', 'HLA-DQA1', 'HLA-DRB1', 'HLA-E', 'IDO1', 'LAG3', 'NKG7', 'PDCD1LG2','PSMB10', 'STAT1', 'TIGIT')
```

```{r}
#Extract 18 genes from DESeq2 resuslts
res_tcell <- res[rownames(res) %in% GEP_genes, ]

res_tcell
```

All 18 genes are present in our dataset

```{r}
res_tcell <- as.data.frame(res_tcell)
```

Genes with an adjusted p-value less than 0.05

```{r}
res_tcell_sig <- res_tcell[
  !is.na(res_tcell$padj) & res_tcell$padj < 0.05,
]

res_tcell_sig
```

Genes with p-value \< 0.05 and log2Foldchange \> 0.5

```{r}
res_tcell_interesting <- res_tcell[
  !is.na(res_tcell$pvalue) &
  res_tcell$pvalue < 0.05 &
  abs(res_tcell$log2FoldChange) > 0.5,
]

res_tcell_interesting

```

### Calculate a T-cell–inflamed GEP score for each patient.

```{r}
# 2. Get transformed expression values from DESeq2
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)
expr <- assay(vsd)

```

```{r}
# 3. Find which genes are present
GEP_genes_present <- GEP_genes[GEP_genes %in% rownames(expr)]

setdiff(GEP_genes, GEP_genes_present)

```

All genes are present

```{r}
# 4. Extract the genes
#Result is matrix of 18 genes and 192 sample columns
GEP_expr <- expr[GEP_genes_present, , drop = FALSE]
GEP_expr
```

```{r}
# 5. Standardize expression for each gene
GEP_expr_scaled <- t(scale(t(GEP_expr)))
GEP_expr_scaled
```

```{r}
# 6. Calculate average expression score per patient
GEP_scores <- colMeans(GEP_expr_scaled, na.rm = TRUE)
GEP_scores
```

```{r}
GEP_df <- data.frame(
  Patient = colnames(expr),
  BOR = colData(dds)$BOR,
  GEP_score = GEP_scores
)
```

A GEP for each sample is shown below:

```{r}
GEP_df
```

A boxplot of how patients respond, based on T-cell-inflamed GEP score

```{r}
boxplot(
  GEP_score ~ BOR,
  data = GEP_df,
  xlab = "Best Overall Response",
  ylab = "T-cell-inflamed GEP score"
)
```

### Investigate whether patients with higher GEP scores are more likely to respond to anti-PD-L1 treatment.

-   **Null hypothesis (H₀):** GEP scores are not associated with treatment response.

-   **Alternative hypothesis (H₁):** Higher GEP scores are associated with a greater likelihood of treatment response.

```{r}
wilcox.test(GEP_score ~ BOR, data = GEP_df)
```

This indicates that we can reject the null hypothesis, and that higher GEP seems to be associated with a greater likelihood of treatment response.

```{r}
GEP_df$Response <- ifelse(
  GEP_df$BOR == "R", 1, 0
)
```

Using logistic regression to further confirm results

```{r}
model <- glm(
  Response ~ GEP_score,
  data = GEP_df,
  family = binomial
)

summary(model)
```

Shows a p-value of 0.0005, which is well below 0.05. This further confirms the alternative hypothesis.

```{r}
exp(coef(model))
```

This is the odds ratio. It shows that for every one-unit increase in GEP scores, the estimated odds of responding to treatment are approximately 3.02 ties as high.

```{r}
exp(confint.default(model))
```

### Interpret the biological significance of your findings and discuss why a high T- cell–inflamed GEP score does not necessarily guarantee treatment response

A high T-cell-inflamed GEP score indicates an immune-inflamed tumor environment; this is not equal to treatment response, but might indicate whether patients are more likely to respond. Other immunosuppressive mechanisms may be active, or tumor cells may escape recognition.
